source.anchor_kjv: They part my garments among them, and cast lots upon my vesture.
source.thread: Psalm 22:18, written ~1000 years early, names TWO acts a dying man's executioners would do — divide his garments AND cast lots for them; John 19:24 records the soldiers at Jesus' cross doing exactly both and cites this verse as fulfilled.
source.hook_line: Ten centuries before the cross, a song recorded exactly how a dying man's clothes would be divided up.
source.spoken_script: Ten centuries before the cross, a song recorded exactly how a dying man's clothes would be divided up. Psalm 22. David wrote it in the first person, but David himself was never executed. He died an old man. He was describing someone else. Stripped, surrounded, his life poured out. Watch one line. He wrote that the dying man's killers would divide his clothes and cast lots for them. They part my garments among them and cast lots upon my vesture. A thousand years later, John watched it at the cross, soldiers dividing Jesus's clothes, then casting lots for the seamless coat, that the scripture might be fulfilled. A thousand years early, God had it written down, so when it happened, you'd know the cross was no accident. It was the plan. The suffering man of Psalm 22 has a name, Jesus. They rolled dice for the clothes off his back, never seeing what he was really doing, laying down his life to win you back.

platforms.title: They Cast Lots for His Clothes - Written Down 1,000 Years Before
platforms.description:
Ten centuries before the cross, a psalm recorded exactly how a dying man's executioners would handle his clothes.

Psalm 22:18 (KJV): "They part my garments among them, and cast lots upon my vesture."

Two acts named: dividing the clothes, and casting lots for the seamless coat. A thousand years later, John watched both happen at Calvary - then cited this verse directly.

David was never executed. He died an old man. He was describing someone else.

That someone was Jesus. The soldiers rolled dice for the clothes off his back, never seeing what they were doing. God had it written down a thousand years early so when it happened, you would know the cross was no accident. It was the plan.

platforms.label: YouTube (Long-form 16:9)
platforms.title: Psalm 22 Named the Two Acts the Soldiers Would Do 1,000 Years Before the Cross
platforms.description:
Ten centuries before the cross, a psalm named two specific acts a dying man's executioners would do with his clothes: divide them, and cast lots for them.

Psalm 22:18 (KJV): "They part my garments among them, and cast lots upon my vesture."

David wrote this in the first person - but David was never executed. He died an old man in his palace. He was describing someone else.

A thousand years later, John 19:24 records the soldiers at Jesus' cross doing exactly both - dividing his garments, then casting lots for the seamless coat - and then John cites Psalm 22:18 directly: that the scripture might be fulfilled.

The soldiers had no idea they were fulfilling a prophecy. They were just doing their job.

God had it written down a thousand years early, so when it happened, you would know the cross was no accident. It was the plan. The suffering man of Psalm 22 has a name: Jesus. He laid down his life to win you back.

Psalm 22 | John 19 | KJV

redteam:
VERDICT: REVISE

One real problem; rest is clean.

1. **YouTube Long description — "He died an old man in his palace."**
   "In his palace" is not in 1 Kings 2. The text says David "slept with his fathers" and was buried in the city of David. Adding "in his palace" is a small embellishment the text doesn't support. A careful reader will notice and distrust the broader argument. Fix: "He died an old man, in his bed" or simply "He died an old man" (drop the location).

Everything else checks out:
- KJV quote is verbatim for all platforms that carry it ("They part my garments among them, and cast lots upon my vesture."). ✓
- "Seamless coat" is accurate — John 19:23 calls it "without seam." ✓
- "That the scripture might be fulfilled" is paraphrased, not in quotes, so no KJV-strict trap. ✓
- No em-dashes anywhere. ✓
- No gain/loss or fear framing; CTA is grace-anchored ("laid down his life to win you back"). ✓
- TikTok hook is punchy and accurate on the first line. ✓
- No ToS banlist terms. ✓
- Title is specific and honest — "written down 1,000 years before" is historically supportable. ✓
- YouTube Short and Facebook correctly avoid all partial-quote traps. ✓

Minimum fix: change "He died an old man in his palace" to "He died an old man" in the YouTube Long description.
